reasoning: This is a narrative literature review synthesizing existing research on schizophrenia cognition, aetiology, pathophysiology and treatment. It does not generate or use any research software, nor does it generate or analyze any new research dataset; it only cites and discusses findings from other published studies.

This is a consensus guideline paper that synthesizes existing literature (systematic reviews, case reports, case series, RCTs) to produce clinical recommendations for managing catatonia. It does not generate or use any research software - there is no mention of code, tools, or computational methods developed or employed. It also does not generate new research data nor substantively use an existing dataset for novel analysis; rather it reviews and cites findings from previously published studies to inform expert consensus recommendations. No datasets are analyzed, no software is described, and no new data collection occurred as part of this guideline development.

The researchers used existing research software (TopoToolbox V2, and ArcGIS Web AppBuilder) to process a nationwide IfSAR DEM, but did not create or significantly extend any software themselves—TopoToolbox was applied with standard algorithms. This constitutes Software Used (S2). They generated a new national-scale geodatabase of 91 morphometric and topographic characteristics for 128 river catchments, which is a novel research dataset created through their workflow and made available via a web-application—this constitutes Data Generated (D1).

The paper develops a new visualization tool (MGDrawVis), implementing the Jaya algorithm (novel application to graph drawing) along with Hill Climbing and Simulated Annealing for comparison - this is genuinely created research software that generates new knowledge (first application of Jaya to graph drawing, LHS-enhanced variant). The software and code are shared via OSF. Additionally, the research generates substantial new data: synthetic random graphs (Erdős–Rényi generated datasets across multiple phases and scalability tests) and experimental result datasets (objective function values, evaluation counts, timing data) produced through the experiments. While some real-world graph datasets (dolphins, karate club, etc.) were used from external sources, the paper's primary contribution involves generated software (Jaya-based tool) and generated data (synthetic benchmark graphs and experimental results), justifying S1D1.

This is a research protocol for a planned randomised clinical trial (ERiC) that has not yet reported results or actual data collection/analysis outcomes. The software mentioned (R for random number generation, REDCap for data management) are standard utility tools used for administrative/logistical purposes (randomization, data capture) rather than research software generating new knowledge themselves. No actual dataset is presented, analysed, or generated as findings in this paper - it only describes planned data collection procedures, measures, and a statistical analysis plan for a trial that just began recruitment. Per the criteria, protocols describing planned data/software use (not yet executed with reported results) should be classified as S3D3 unless there is clear evidence of actual data or software-generated findings reported in the paper itself.

The paper reports an original survey study: researchers developed competency questions via literature review and interviews, then surveyed four cohorts of nurses/midwives (n=153) to generate new quantitative (Likert scale) and qualitative (thematic) data on confidence and perceived importance of genomics competencies. This constitutes newly generated research data (survey responses, interview transcripts) used to produce novel findings. No research software was created or used for scientific knowledge generation - analysis was done with standard tools (Microsoft Excel, standard statistical tests like t-test, ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis) which are generic utilities, not research software developed or substantively used to generate new knowledge. Hence S3 (no research software) and D1 (data generated).

This is an editorial/special issue overview article that summarizes and reviews seven accepted papers using a quality assessment scale (MQAS). It does not itself generate or use any research software or research data; it merely describes/evaluates other papers' contributions. No software was created or used by this editorial, and no new/existing research data was generated or analyzed by the authors of this piece itself.

The paper uses existing software tools (NiftyReg for registration, Varian Eclipse TPS for treatment planning) as utilities to generate new knowledge (TCP maps, dose escalation plans) without creating or substantially extending any new research software - these are standard clinical/research tools used as-is. For data, the paper uses patient DW-MRI/ADC and CT imaging data collected from 10 GBM patients treated with radiotherapy - this is existing clinical patient data (retrospective cohort) that is used to derive cell density and TCP maps, rather than newly generated research data as the primary contribution. The ADC-cell density relationship formula is also borrowed from a previously published study (Eidel et al.) rather than generated. The study is an in-silico simulation using existing patient imaging data and existing software tools to produce novel treatment planning insights.

The paper describes development of an "innovative multiplexed immunofluorescence and digital image analysis workflow" with custom phenotyping steps (dynamic image thresholding, colocalisation-based resolution algorithms) implemented in open-source software specifically for this research, generating new knowledge (cell phenotype quantification) - this constitutes generated research software (S1). The study also generated new primary research data: archival tissue samples were stained, imaged via multiplexed immunofluorescence to produce millions of phenotyped cell detections across hundreds of histological images - a novel dataset created specifically for this study to characterize immune microenvironments across NLPHL/THRLBCL spectrum, qualifying as generated research data (D1).

The researchers manually coded the GMDH neural network steps in MATLAB rather than using an existing research software package or toolbox (MATLAB itself is a general computational utility, not research software created for this research with lasting reusable identity, and no toolbox was used/generated beyond ad hoc implementation of a known algorithm). This coding is essentially implementing a known algorithm (GMDH, from 1968) as a utility to analyze the data, not creating new reusable research software with novel capabilities - it's a straightforward implementation used as an analysis tool. The data used (384 survey responses via BRCS, MBI-GS, and custom Covid-19 stress questionnaire) was actually gathered from a previous study referenced as [31], making this existing/used data rather than newly generated data for this specific paper. The paper states "The information utilized in this study was gathered from previous research [31]," indicating the dataset was reused from prior work, fitting D2 (Data Used) rather than D1 (Data Generated). Since no distinct reusable research software artifact was created (just an algorithm implementation for analysis use), and the data was substantively used from existing sources to produce new findings, this fits S3D2.

The paper reports new experimental data generated in the research: a novel crystal structure of Mcl-1 bound to AMG-176 (deposited in PDB as 8AV9), NMR solution structures/HSQC data, SPR binding affinities, and free-ligand conformer analyses. These are newly generated research data that produce new knowledge about the mechanism of PPI inhibition. The software/tools mentioned (PP scoring, PLB index, ECHOS-NMR analysis, MD/DFT computations) are used as standard analysis utilities/established methods rather than software created or substantially extended by the authors for this study, so no new research software is generated. Thus the paper fits S3 (no research software generated) and D1 (research data generated).

This is a cluster RCT in rural South Africa that generated new primary research data through surveys, interviews, anthropometric measurements, and medical record review of 873 mother-child pairs across 8 clinics. The data (maternal/child outcomes, EPDS scores, growth measurements, ARV adherence, etc.) were newly collected for this study, constituting generated research data (D1). While the paper mentions using the 'blme' R package for statistical modeling, this is a standard statistical software tool used for routine data analysis rather than research software developed or substantively created for this study - it's a utility package, placing it in S3 (no research software generated/used in a substantive sense).

The study uses existing EHR databases (UK Biobank and CPRD Gold, both pre-existing research data sources) linked to cancer registry data to analyze symptom/test rates. No new research software was created - they developed clinical code 'phenotypes' (codelists mapping symptom concepts to Read v2/CTV3 codes), which are classification schemas rather than software/code artifacts, and used standard statistical methods (Poisson models) rather than developing novel software tools. No new primary data was generated; the research substantively used existing secondary data (EHR records) to produce new knowledge about differences in symptom recording between cohorts, qualifying as Data Used (D2). Hence S3D2.

This is a perspective/opinion piece discussing decolonisation of the psychology curriculum, synthesizing literature, historical accounts, and existing frameworks. It does not involve any software development or use, nor does it generate or use any research data (datasets, corpora, etc.). It is a conceptual/discursive review without empirical data collection or computational tools.

This is a Scientific Data paper describing the compilation of a new global dataset (DOCU-CLIM) of 621 documentary climate time series, created by compiling existing sources, rescuing historical data, and digitizing new series. This constitutes substantive research data generation. While R-code is mentioned to read the files and regression models were fit for forward modeling, these are standard statistical utility tools (R scripts, least-squares regression) rather than newly developed research software that itself generates new knowledge beyond being a utility for data processing/analysis. No new software package or tool is presented as a contribution; the paper's focus and novel contribution is the dataset itself.

The study generated novel research data: sedimentary archive sampling, multilocus metabarcoding (eDNA) sequencing data across 100 years, mass spectrometry chemical quantification, and compiled climate/biocide records - all newly produced for this research, qualifying as D1 (Data Generated). For software, the paper uses existing established research software/tools (QIIME2, DADA2, PICRUST2, ANCOM, cutadapt, FASTQC, ggplot2, pheatmap, sCCA methods) to analyze the data, but does not report creating or substantially extending any new software tool. Hence it falls under S2 (Software Used) for the computational analysis pipeline. Combined, this corresponds to S2D1.

This is a narrative/state-of-the-art review article discussing imaging techniques for blood-brain barrier dysfunction across various neurological diseases. It synthesizes existing literature on PET, SPECT, MRI (DCE, ASL), and CT imaging methods without generating or using specific research software or datasets. No new software tools were developed, no existing research software was applied to generate results, and no research data (datasets, corpora, patient cohorts) were created or analyzed. The paper is purely a literature review/synthesis for clinical education purposes.

The study generated new survey data through a cross-sectional survey of 10,007 respondents in Malang, Indonesia, using a questionnaire on COVID-19 knowledge and vaccine uptake. This is clearly substantive research data generated by the study, creating new knowledge about knowledge-vaccine uptake associations. Regarding software, the paper mentions using KoboToolbox (an existing data collection app) for survey administration and STATA 17.1 for statistical analysis - both are standard utility tools used for data collection and analysis, not research software created or substantively extended for generating new knowledge themselves. No new software was developed; existing tools were used in a routine capacity.

This is a narrative review article discussing published GWAS, post-GWAS, and functional studies on AD and PD genetics and microglia biology. The authors synthesize and discuss existing literature (tools like FUMA, MAGMA, DeepSea, CADD, sLDSC are mentioned only as examples of methods used in cited studies, not used or created by the authors themselves), but do not generate or use any software or data themselves as part of new research conducted in this paper. No new datasets, software, or analyses were produced; it is purely a literature synthesis/review.

This is a narrative review article summarizing existing literature on MAIT cells and the microbiome. It does not report any new software development/use or generation/use of new research data by the authors themselves; rather, it synthesizes findings from previously published primary studies (cited as references) without conducting new experiments, analyses, or data collection. No software tools are described as being created or used for analysis in this paper, and no new datasets are generated or substantively reused/analyzed. Hence it falls into S3D3 (no research software, no research data).

The authors developed a novel counterfactual GAN architecture (adapted/modified from Choi et al.'s framework) specifically for generating synthetic longitudinal OCT retinal images, along with referee neural networks for evaluation - this constitutes genuine software generation that produces new knowledge (the counterfactual images and insights about retinal aging). The data used (UK Biobank OCT images) is an existing, pre-collected dataset that the researchers used but did not generate themselves - it was acquired as part of the UK Biobank population study, not created by this research. Thus this is S1 (software generated) and D2 (data used, not generated).

The paper generates simulated narratives using GPT-2 with modified parameters (temperature, memory span) and custom text-generation pipeline/scripts (beam-search sampling configurations, nucleus sampling, 2-gram repetition prevention, preprocessing pipeline), accompanied by a hands-on Python tutorial - this constitutes research software created for the research purpose (a novel simulation framework), generating new knowledge about NLP metric validity. The simulated narratives themselves (1200+ generated texts, plus clinician ratings on 249 narratives) constitute newly generated research data used to validate NLP measures - this is substantive data created specifically for this study rather than pre-existing data. Since both software and data were generated, the paper falls into S1D1 per the rule that generation supersedes mere use when both occur.

This is a study protocol describing a planned international survey; the survey has not yet been conducted and no data has been collected or analyzed yet. Software (Qualtrics XM) is mentioned only as a planned utility tool for survey distribution, not as research software generating new knowledge. Since the data collection and analysis are prospective/planned rather than already executed, and no actual dataset or software artifact is produced in this paper, it falls under S3D3 (no software generated/used for research purposes, no data generated/used yet - only planned).

This is a clinical phase 1 pharmacokinetic drug-drug interaction study that generated new experimental data (PK concentration measurements, AUC/Cmax values from human subjects) specifically for this research, constituting research data generation (D1). The software used (Phoenix WinNonlin for noncompartmental PK analysis, SAS for statistics) are standard analytical/statistical utility tools used for routine data analysis rather than research software created or substantively extended for this study - they are applied as off-the-shelf computational tools, not generating new knowledge themselves beyond standard calculations (S3).

This paper describes a methodology paper operationalizing a standardized scoring system using existing UK Biobank data (anthropometric, physical activity, dietary data from touchscreen questionnaire and 24h dietary assessments). No new research software was created - they used standard calculations/formulas (e.g., BMI formula) and existing questionnaires/tools (IPAQ, Oxford WebQ) which are utilities rather than generated research software. The data used (UK Biobank) is existing research data that was not generated by this study; the paper computes scores on existing data to enable future analyses, which counts as "Data Used" (D2) rather than generated, since UK Biobank data collection predates and is independent of this study. No software was generated or substantively used as a research tool beyond standard statistical/arithmetic calculations.

This is a narrative literature review discussing existing cardiovascular risk scores, biomarkers, and ocular imaging studies from the literature. It does not generate or substantively use any new research software (it references software/apps used in cited studies like Brennan et al., but does not itself develop or run analyses using software), nor does it generate or analyze any new research data itself - it synthesizes findings from previously published papers. No new datasets or software artifacts are produced or substantively used within this paper.

The study uses existing software (Google Trends platform and the Joinpoint Regression Programme) to analyze data, but does not create or extend any software itself - these are used as analytical tools/utilities, though the Joinpoint software is substantively used to generate new findings (joinpoint analysis results), classifying as S2. For data, the researchers downloaded existing Google Trends search volume data (RSV) and CDC case data - pre-existing data sources that were not generated by the research but used substantively to produce new knowledge about information-seeking patterns, making it D2 (Data Used).

This is a qualitative interview-based study where the researchers generated original research data by conducting in-depth interviews with 30 Dental Officers and 17 Dental Managers, transcribing and thematically analyzing the data to derive new themes/findings on COVID-19's impact on dental service delivery in Fiji. This constitutes generated research data (D1), as new qualitative data was collected and is the core source of new knowledge in the paper. No research software was created or used substantively; analysis was manual thematic analysis using Microsoft Word for transcription, which is a routine utility tool, not research software that generates new knowledge (S3).

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis that synthesizes data extracted from 76 previously published articles and national surveys (DHS, national micronutrient survey) on adolescent nutrition in Ethiopia - this is clearly 'Research Data Used' (D2) since the data (extracted study data, prevalence estimates) was pre-existing from other published studies, not newly generated by the authors' own primary data collection. The authors used STATA version 17, an existing statistical software package, to perform the meta-analysis (random effects model, forest plots) - this is 'Software Used' (S2) since STATA is a standard pre-existing statistical tool used to analyze the data, not software created by the researchers. There is no indication that new software was developed for this research; STATA was used as a utility/tool to generate the meta-analytic findings (pooled prevalence estimates), which does constitute substantive analysis generating new synthesized knowledge, hence S2 rather than S3.

This paper reports a new empirical study collecting HD-EMG and force data from TD and DCD children, generating novel research data (motor unit firing characteristics) that forms the core new knowledge of the paper - classifying as D1 (Data Generated). The software used (NeuroMap/Delsys proprietary decomposition software, Labchart, Matlab scripts, PsychoPy) are existing tools/utilities used to collect and process data rather than research software created or substantively extended by the authors - the Matlab script is described as "bespoke" but used only for routine data extraction/analysis, not as a novel methodological contribution generating new knowledge itself. Thus S3 (No Research Software) applies.
